title: The wall that heals itself
question: Why Has Roman Concrete Survived for 2,000 Years?
scoredBy: inspection of rendered frames at 0/33/66/94 per shot
verdict: The best script of the five and the worst match to the engine. The whole episode is about a MECHANISM -- a crack opens, water reaches a lime clast, the lime recrystallises across the gap and seals it -- and not one frame shows it. Twenty-three shots, twenty-three of them typography. A viewer finishes knowing the fact and having seen nothing that would let them check it.
whatWorked: The script's reversal is genuinely good: the lumps we read as sloppy work are the repair system.
green-rot over the drawn ground is the one mood of the five that produces a usable frame without a photograph -- dark olive with pale gold type reads as a document rather than as an empty slide.
The route motif drawing an arc on the 'crack' line is the closest the reel gets to showing a process.
The closing card -- TWO THOUSAND, years and still curing -- is well made.

whatFailed.what: The self-healing mechanism, which is the entire subject, is never drawn.
whatFailed.why: chooseRepresentation has gearSystem, timeline, measurement, orbit and scan. A chemical process that closes a gap matches none of them, so the strongest available representation for the episode's central claim was a sentence.

whatFailed.what: Zero diagrams in fifty seconds; the image kind never changes.
whatFailed.why: Same cause. The editor reports 'the reel changes its kind of image 0 times in 23 shots'.

whatFailed.what: '40 BC' and 'the first century' never became a timeline.
whatFailed.why: yearsIn only recognises four-digit years, so a BC date and a named century are invisible to the one diagram type that would have fitted this episode.

whatFailed.what: A wire prop and the slate land on the same frame in shot 0.
whatFailed.why: Two arrivals sharing a moment read as one beat; the opening shot has one event, not two.

gatesFailed: no photograph anywhere in the reel — every shot is drawn or typeset
